# The Man Led by a Woman {#the-man-led-by-a-woman}

> "He followed her immediately, as an ox goes to the slaughter"
>
> — Proverbs 7:22

Some men use women. This chapter is about the man who gets used. He would tell you that he is only being good to her. The slang of the 2020s calls it simping. A man wants a woman so badly that she can lead him anywhere, and so can anyone else who knows what he wants. The word is new. The problem is very old. The Bible tells it twice, once about the strongest man who ever lived and once about a king.

## Samson and Delilah {-}

The strong man is Samson, in the book of Judges. He was the strongest man who ever lived. God gave him that strength to free his people from their enemies, the Philistines, and no army could hold him. His weakness was women, and his enemies knew it. He fell in love with a woman named Delilah, and the Philistine rulers came to her with an offer. "Entice him, and see in which his great strength lies." Each of them promised her eleven hundred pieces of silver.

Three times she asked him for his secret. Three times he told her a lie, and each time she tried it on him with armed men hiding in the next room.

Stop there and look at him. Three times this woman has tried to hand him to men who want him dead. He knows it. And he stays. That is what lust does to a strong man's judgment. He isn't fooled. He just can't leave.

Then she used the oldest line there is. "How can you say, 'I love you,' when your heart is not with me?" She "pressed him daily with her words" until he was worn out, and at last he told her the truth. His strength was tied to a vow of dedication to God, and its sign was that his hair had never been cut. She put him to sleep on her knees, called a man to shave his head, and collected her silver.

## At the mill {-}

So the strongest man alive was sold for silver by the woman he couldn't leave. He woke up sure that he would shake himself free as before. "But he didn't know that the LORD had departed from him." The Philistines put out his eyes, the eyes that had led him all his life, "and he ground at the mill in the prison".

But the story doesn't end at the mill. The very next line reads, "However, the hair of his head began to grow again".

At a great feast the Philistine rulers had him brought up from the prison to entertain them. A boy led him by the hand to the pillars that held the building up. Then he prayed. "Lord GOD, remember me, please, and strengthen me, please, only this once". God heard him. The temple came down on the rulers and on Samson himself.

It isn't a tidy ending. He never got back his sight or the wasted years. But God heard a ruined man when he asked, and gave him back the work he was born for.

If you have been at the mill for years, he still hears that prayer.

## The king who sold himself {-}

Samson was led by a woman he wanted. The king was led by the woman he had. He was King Ahab, and he let his wife Jezebel, a ruthless woman, run him. When he sulked over a vineyard its owner wouldn't sell, she had the owner killed in the king's name, and Ahab went and took the vineyard. The Bible says he "sold himself". A prophet confronted him, and he was sorry for a while. Then he went on as before.

Being sorry is not the same as turning around.

And notice where both stories put the blame. Delilah was paid and Jezebel was ruthless. But Samson gave away his own secret, and Ahab let his own name be used. A man ruled by what he wants ends up ruled by whoever can give it to him.

## The man who buys the drinks {-}

Those are old stories, but the man in them hasn't gone anywhere. There's one you may recognize at any party. He walks in and goes straight to the women. He doesn't say hello to the men. He buys a round, and every glass goes to a girl. He would tell you he is just a generous, friendly guy.

Here is the test. Does he buy the men a drink? Does he spend as much time talking to the men? A generous man is generous with everybody. This man is spending, and he knows what he is shopping for. What makes the difference is what he intends.

Now look at the free man in the same room. He can see that a woman is beautiful. It simply stops deciding anything. He doesn't buy the drink or laugh at the joke that wasn't funny. He doesn't give her the favor, the job or the last word because of her face. He treats her as he treats everyone else, which is fairly.

That is better for him. He keeps his money, his judgment and his self-respect. It is better for her too, because she gets dealt with as a person. And it is better for the plain woman standing beside her, whom thirsty men have looked straight through all her life.

## The lever at home {-}

That is the free man at a party, among women he will never see again. It matters far more with the woman he lives with. There's a man who gives in on everything. When his partner is unfair to him, or plainly out of line, he says nothing, because he is afraid of what it will cost him that night. Sex has become a lever in that house. Some women pull that lever on purpose, and that is wrong of them. Others never give it a thought. But he can't change her. What he can change is whether the lever works.

Now take the man whose lust no longer runs him. He can say, quite calmly, "That isn't right, and I won't go along with it." If she tells him he can sleep on the couch tonight, he picks up a pillow and goes. To him it feels like camping.

He isn't being cold, and he isn't punishing her. He still loves her, and he still wants her. But he can't be bought with it, and he can't be starved with it, so he is free to tell her the truth. That is better for her as well. She can trust his yes, because he is a man who is able to say no.

Samson was the strongest man alive, and Ahab was a king, and neither of them could say no to a woman. The man with the pillow under his arm is neither strong nor a king. He is only free, and that turns out to be the one thing that matters. Nobody can lead him by what he wants, because it no longer leads him.
